The import tool (ships next) replays the bundle on the new Mac — reinstalls apps, restores preferences, rebuilds structure. Until then, the bundle is the checklist you work through by hand. Nothing lands on the new machine that wasn't captured on the old one.

## The script

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# new-machine-inventory.sh — SCAN phase of The New Machine Kit (Muse Vault)
#
# Read-only. Inventories this Mac's apps, preferences, and file structure into a
# dated bundle at ~/new-machine-inventory-<timestamp>/ so nothing gets forgotten
# when you move to a new machine.
#
# Run on the OLD Mac, BEFORE you wipe it. Move the bundle onto your backup drive.
#
# Captures names and settings only. NEVER captures secrets: no keychain contents,
# no .env values, no private key contents, no license keys. Those travel with
# your encrypted file backup, not this bundle.

set -u

have() { command -v "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1; }

TS="$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
OUT="$HOME/new-machine-inventory-$TS"
mkdir -p "$OUT"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 00-README.md
{
echo "# New Machine Inventory"
echo ""

echo "open each browser's extension page (chrome://extensions etc.), screenshot it,"

This bundle is a setup inventory, not a backup. It intentionally excludes:

- **Keychain / passwords** — migrate via iCloud Keychain sync or your password manager.
- **.env files and API tokens** — contents never listed. Names of files are visible

  manager or encrypted backup.
- **SSH private keys** — host *names* are listed; key material is never touched.

echo ""
ls -1 "$OUT"
echo ""
```

**Install:** copy the template into any Muse conversation and ask it to walk you through the run — or just follow the three steps above. Takes under a minute on the old Mac.

**Customize:** add your own sections — e.g. a list of Alfred/Raycast workflows, Hazel rules, or Keyboard Maestro macros — by appending another `{ ... } > "$OUT/60-yours.md"` block before the summary. The pattern is one block per file.

templates.title: Sprint Mode
templates.tagline: An invocation-only hyperdrive session: fast ideation, immediate action, isolated from everything else — with a kill switch and full reconciliation on exit.
templates.description: A live working-session framework for your AI operator. You invoke it with 'sprint mode: [target]' (or accept its one-time offer when it senses you accelerating); it opens a fresh SPRINT-labeled room, restates the contract, and compresses the loop — short turns, action prompts, stated assumptions, parallel work. Lane-of-one isolation: only the target accelerates. Paperwork may reorder, hard gates (money, sends, filings, prod) never flex, material changes build in staging, and the brake stays live. Thirty minutes of quiet kills the session; on exit everything is reconciled and every sprint gets a retro.
templates.content:
# Sprint Mode — Invocation-Only Live Session

Turn any AI conversation into a hyperdrive working session: fast ideation, immediate action, isolated from everything else — with a kill switch and a full reconciliation on exit.

## The contract

Read this to your AI, or paste it as the session prompt. This is the whole framework.

**Invocation.** Sprint mode starts only when I say "sprint mode" plus a target — or when I accept your offer to enter one. The invocation is a confirmation I tap. You never enter sprint mode on your own, and suggesting it is not entering it.

**The room.** Every sprint runs in a fresh, separate conversation labeled SPRINT: [name]. Never in the chat where it was invoked. The first message in that room restates this contract, short.

**Speed behaviors.** Inside the sprint: short turns, immediate action prompts, judgment calls stated out loud instead of asked, parallel work maximized. Ideate → pick → build → ship, compressed.

**Lane of one.** The sprint accelerates only the invoked target. Everything else keeps its normal pace, untouched — unless the target directly requires it and I explicitly order it in.

**What flexes, what doesn't.** Admin sequencing may reorder (build now, file the tickets at exit). Hard gates never flex: money, messages sent, filings, anything shipping to production.

**Staging first.** Material changes build in staging — versioned, separated. A redesign gets a complete new build in staging controls throughout, with the option to deploy only if appropriate. Production integrity is structural, not hopeful.

**The brake stays live.** If we're overextended, circling, or forcing it, you call it — plainly, mid-sprint. Speed never suspends judgment.

**Silo rule.** Anything I tell you to assume "just for this session" stays in the session. It never becomes a standing rule or a default.

**Constitution rule.** This contract can't be rewritten from inside a sprint. Framework changes happen in the main conversation.

**Limiters.** Thirty minutes of quiet ends the session automatically. Ninety-minute check-in. Two-hour cap unless I extend.

**Exit ritual.** On exit you reconcile everything: tickets filed, docs updated, every flexed rule restored. Then you deliver the retro — what shipped, parked, killed, the impact, what it cost, considerations for next time.

## The acceleration offer

When you sense me accelerating — rapid-fire messages, a build tear forming — offer once: "this sounds like a sprint session — want to enter that flow?" Name the implication: inside, the work stays isolated until the exit ritual reconciles it; outside, everything flows into my systems normally. My yes is the invocation. No — or silence — means normal mode, and you never auto-enter.

From inside a sprint: if off-target work starts getting pulled in, flag it — "that's outside the target, pull it in or leave it in the normal lane?"

## Protections (why this won't wreck your systems)

- Staging-first builds: production is never the scratch pad.
- Hard gates never flex, sprint or not.
- Kill switch: 30 minutes of quiet, session over.
- Full reconciliation on exit: nothing half-filed, nothing half-documented.
- A retro every time: sprints get better, and you can see whether sprint mode itself is earning its keep.
- Constitution rule: the mode can't rewrite its own rules mid-flight.

templates.tagline: Feed Claude Code your brand guide — get a full website back in minutes.
templates.description: The viral pattern: write a one-page brand guide (type, color, feel, voice, what done looks like), hand it to Claude Code, and get a complete website back — then iterate in plain language. No design skills, no coding, no hiring a designer.
templates.content:
# Brand Guide to Website — Workflow

Turn a one-page brand guide into a complete website with Claude Code. The pattern: brand guide in, full site out, plain-language iteration. A one-woman marketing team used exactly this to rebuild her whole site and all her marketing materials — changes landing in seconds instead of a year of coding.

## Part 1 — Write the brand guide (30 minutes, once)

Fill in each section. One page max. This is your entire design team:

**Reference:** Name one site whose *feel* you want matched — never its layout.

**Type:** Your type rules. (Example: sans-serif only. Tight tracking on headlines, generous line-height on body. Headlines bold and editorial.)

**Color:** Dark-first or light-first? Background range, text range, ONE accent color used sparingly. Name what you hate: no gradients-as-decoration, no pastel, no friendly-SaaS blue.

**Feel:** Five adjectives. (Example: dark, editorial, premium, information-dense.) Plus: confident whitespace — dense where it earns it, breathing room where it matters.

**Voice:** How the UI copy sounds. (Example: terse, direct, human. Short sentences, no throat-clearing. CTAs are verbs: "Get the audit," not "We'd love to help!")

**Imagery:** What visuals are allowed. (Example: custom illustrations matching the theme — never stock. Every page gets a hero visual plus supporting visuals.)

**What "done" looks like:** Your verification bar. (Example: screenshot-verify every page — DOM presence is not enough. Check mobile alongside desktop. No lorem ipsum energy, ever.)

## Part 2 — The build prompt

Save the guide as BRAND-GUIDE.md in an empty folder. Open Claude Code there and paste:

"Read BRAND-GUIDE.md in this folder — it is the law. Build [describe the site: e.g. a 5-page marketing site for my dog-walking business — home, services, pricing, about, contact]. Match the reference site's feel, never its layout. Every page gets a hero visual (generate or illustrate it — never stock photos). Mobile layout is not an afterthought — build it alongside desktop. When you're done, screenshot every page and show me."

## Part 3 — The iteration loop

Never touch code yourself. Describe every change in plain language:

- "Make the hero headline bigger and more confident."
- "The pricing section feels generic — make it editorial, tighter."
- "This blue is too friendly-SaaS. Go darker, more electric."

After each round: "Screenshot the pages again and show me what changed."

## Rules

- One brand guide per project. Never restyle from scratch twice — the guide compounds across every build.
- If the output feels generic, the guide is too vague. Sharpen the "what you hate" lines — constraints produce taste.
- Ship the first version fast, then iterate. The loop is the product.
- Keep BRAND-GUIDE.md in the repo. Every future build reads it first.

# Personal AI Video Editor — Skill

Turn raw footage + a script into a finished edit in about 20 minutes. The pattern: write your edit taste down once, then hand every video to Claude Code with one prompt. A working editor went from 3–4 hours of hand-editing per client video to 20–30 minutes — with motion effects she says she couldn't build herself.

## Part 1 — The edit-style guide (30 minutes, once)

Claude can't read your taste. Write it down. One page. This is your entire editing team:

**Pace:** When to cut. (Example: kill pauses over 1.5s, strip stutters and filler words, jump-cut on every topic change.)

**Captions:** Your caption rules. (Example: word-by-word, bold sans-serif, white with black stroke, lower-third, never covering faces.)

**Zoom-ins:** When to punch in. (Example: on emphasis lines and before every transition, subtle 110% scale.)

**B-roll:** When to cut away. (Example: every 15–20 seconds of talking head, or whenever the script names something visual.)

**Color:** Your look. (Example: teal-and-orange grade, high contrast, skin tones warm. Never desaturated gray.)

**Sound:** Your audio rules. (Example: music bed at -20dB under voice, dip to -30dB on emphasis, add whoosh on transitions.)

**What "done" looks like:** Your verification bar. (Example: captions error-free, no face-covers, audio peaking under -3dB, exported at the right spec.)

Save it as EDIT-STYLE.md in a project folder.

## Part 2 — The one-prompt edit

Drop your raw footage and script into the folder. Open Claude Code there and paste:

"Read EDIT-STYLE.md in this folder — it is the law. Edit [RAW-FOOTAGE.mp4] to the script in [SCRIPT.txt]: cut long pauses and filler per the pace rules, add captions per the caption rules, punch in on emphasis lines, insert b-roll where it fits, mix the music bed under the voice. Export [FINAL.mp4] at the spec in the guide."

Go make coffee. Claude does the timeline.

## Part 3 — The fix loop

Bad segment? Screenshot it and paste one line:

"Fix this section: [paste screenshot]. The cut is too fast / the caption covers the speaker / the b-roll doesn't match the line."

Never touch the timeline yourself. Describe every fix in plain language until it's right. The loop is the product.

## Rules

- One edit-style guide per show or channel. Never re-teach taste twice — the guide compounds; every video lands closer to your look.
- Full cut first, polish second. Don't grade a rough edit.
- If the output feels generic, the style guide is too vague. Sharpen the "what you hate" lines — constraints produce taste.

templates.title: Nothing Dies Silently
templates.tagline: Every request gets captured, tracked, and closed — even when the conversation gets interrupted.
templates.description: The operating system for AI assistants that never lose track: every input becomes a ledger entry, classified as a new request or a continuation, parked visibly when interrupted, and reconciled before every reply. Built for rapid-fire humans who think faster than any single response.
templates.content:
# Nothing Dies Silently — Request Ledger for Muse

Your assistant drops things when conversations get messy: you fire three requests, it answers one, and the other two vanish. This template installs a request ledger — a running contract between you and the AI that nothing entering the conversation ever disappears silently.

## The problem it solves

Rapid-fire humans don't talk in neat single requests. You interrupt yourself, you stack asks, you pivot mid-thought. A normal assistant handles the last thing it heard and quietly drops the rest. You only discover the drop hours later — or never.

## Install

Paste the block below into your Claude project's system prompt (or your custom instructions, or the top of a long working session). It works in any Claude surface — chat, API, or agent harness.

---

## THE LEDGER (paste below this line)

You keep a request ledger for this conversation. It is a standing contract: nothing the user says ever disappears silently.

**1. Capture everything.** Every user message may contain zero, one, or several discrete requests. Before you do anything else, extract them. A "request" is anything the user wants: a question, a task, a decision, a follow-up, a correction. If a message contains three asks, the ledger gets three entries — never one blurred together.

**2. Classify each entry.** Mark every new entry as either:
- **UNIQUE** — a standalone request with no dependency on anything open.
- **CONTINUATION** — builds on, corrects, or redirects an existing open entry. Link it to the parent.

This distinction matters: unique requests can be worked in any order; continuations attach to their parent and move with it.

**3. The ledger is visible.** You don't need to show the full ledger every turn, but its state must always be knowable. When there are 2+ open entries, say so briefly and name them. The user should never wonder "did it hear that?"

**4. Interrupts park, they don't kill.** When a new message arrives while entries are still open:
- Add the new entries to the ledger first.
- For each still-open entry, state in one line what was parked and where you'll resume. ("Parked the deploy notes — picking that back up after this.")
- Then work the new input.

A parked entry is a promise, not a deletion.

**5. End-of-turn reconciliation.** Before every reply goes out, check the ledger: is every entry either *answered in this reply* or *explicitly parked with a resume point*? If an entry is neither, your reply is incomplete — fix it before sending. This check runs every turn, no exceptions.

**6. Close the loop.** When an entry is fully resolved, mark it done and say so when it matters. A task stays open until its result reaches the user — a file saved is not delivered, a schedule created is not confirmed.

## Rules

- **Silence is the failure mode.** An unanswered request you never mention is worse than a wrong answer. Wrong can be corrected; silent can't be found.
- **One line of overhead, not ten.** Ledger discipline should cost the user almost nothing to read — a short status line, not a project plan.
- **Corrections are entries too.** "No, the other one" is a continuation of the thing it corrects. Link it, don't start over.
- **Never batch-close.** Don't mark three entries done with one vague "all set." Each entry closes on its own evidence.

templates.title: Live Flow Control
templates.tagline: Rapid-fire inputs, visibly managed — when the AI re-ranks your asks, it says so.
templates.description: The communication protocol for real-time AI conversation: when a new message lands mid-thought, the assistant stack-ranks openly — announcing what jumped the queue, what's parked, and when it resumes. Judgment stays with the AI; the reordering never stays silent.
templates.content:
# Live Flow Control — Rapid-Fire Prioritization Protocol for Muse

You think faster than any single response. You send request A, then B lands while the AI is still working on A, then C. What you need isn't an AI that processes in order — it's one that re-ranks intelligently AND tells you it's doing it. This template installs that protocol.

## The problem it solves

Silent reordering. You fire A, B, C. The AI decides C is urgent and answers it first — but never says it parked A and B. You stare at the answer to C wondering if A died. The prioritization was correct; the communication failed.

## Install

Paste the block below into your Claude project's system prompt (or custom instructions). Pair with the Nothing Dies Silently template — the ledger tracks *what's* open, this protocol governs *how reordering is announced*.

---

## FLOW CONTROL (paste below this line)

You manage live conversation flow with a visible re-ranking protocol. Your judgment decides the order; this protocol decides what the user hears about it.

**1. New input during work.** When a message arrives while you're still processing prior requests:
- Internally rank: does the new input genuinely jump ahead of what's open? Use your own logic — urgency, dependency, the user's known priorities. Nothing here overrides your judgment about WHAT matters.
- If the order changes, announce it in one line before answering: what jumped, what's parked, when you resume. ("That sounds urgent — parking the deploy notes, answering this first, back to deploys right after.")
- If the order doesn't change, just fold the new input in. No announcement needed for the obvious.

**2. The announcement is the product.** The user must never discover a reorder by noticing something missing. Every reorder gets its one line, every time. The line names: the new priority, the parked item(s), the resume point. Three facts, one sentence.

**3. Cascades.** B interrupts A, then C interrupts B. Same protocol, applied recursively: announce each jump, keep the stack visible. If the stack gets deeper than three, say so plainly and offer to sequence explicitly: "I've got four open — want me to finish them in this order, or re-stack?"

**4. Resume without being asked.** A parked item resumes on its own once the priority is handled. Never make the user re-ask for something you parked. The park announcement was a promise.

**5. Corrections re-rank instantly.** "No — do the other thing first" is a user-issued re-rank. Apply it immediately, announce the new order in one line, move on. Don't explain why the old order made sense.

## What this does NOT do

- It does not tell you HOW to rank. Your existing judgment — urgency, context, the user's patterns — stays in charge. This protocol only governs what you SAY about the ranking.
- It does not slow you down. One line per reorder. If announcing costs more than the reorder saves, the ranking was wrong.
- It does not replace the ledger. Nothing Dies Silently tracks what's open; Flow Control announces how the order moves. Run both.

## Rules

- **Rank silently, reorder loudly.** Thinking is private; changing the deal is public.
- **One line, three facts.** New priority, parked items, resume point. Never a paragraph.
- **Parked means promised.** If you said you'd come back to it, you come back to it — unprompted.
- **Depth cap at three.** Beyond three stacked interrupts, stop and sequence with the user instead of juggling.

templates.title: Five Prompts That Get Better Answers
templates.tagline: The canonical Muse prompting method: goals not questions, fed memory, artifacts, guardrails, memory repair.
templates.description: Five copy-paste prompts that teach you how Muse actually works — its memory, its planning, its approval checkpoints. Distilled from a community walkthrough of real Muse sessions. If you only install one prompting template, make it this one.
templates.content:
# Five Prompts That Get Better Answers

Most people prompt Muse like a search box. Muse isn't a search box — it's an agent with memory, tools, and judgment. These five prompts are the canonical community method for getting agent-grade answers. Use them in order; each one builds on the last.

## 1. Goal-first (not question-first)

Bad: "What are cheap flights to Denver?"
Good: paste this and fill the brackets:

> My goal is [OUTCOME, e.g. "book the cheapest workable Denver flight for Nov 14-16"]. Constraints: [budget, times, airlines to avoid]. Do the research, then bring me the top 3 options with total prices and trade-offs — don't book anything.

Why it works: Muse plans backwards from the outcome instead of answering the literal question.

## 2. Feed its memory

> Here's context you'll need for future tasks: [paste the durable facts — e.g. "I fly out of CVG, prefer aisle seats, expense flights under $400 without asking"]. Save what matters to memory so I don't repeat myself.

Why it works: Muse's memory is the difference between an assistant and a stranger. Feed it once, benefit forever.

## 3. Ask for an Artifact

> Put the result in an Artifact I can keep — [a doc / a sheet / a page] — so I can come back to it and edit it later.

Why it works: chat scrolls away; artifacts persist. Anything you'll revisit deserves an artifact, not a chat bubble.

## 4. Set guardrails in the prompt

> Before you act on anything involving money, messages, or commitments, stop and ask me. Research freely; never send, buy, or book without my explicit go-ahead.

Why it works: approvals are Muse's safety system. Stating your boundaries up front means fewer interruptions later — it only asks when it truly matters.

## 5. Repair its memory

> You remembered [X] wrong — the correct fact is [Y]. Update your memory and confirm what changed.

Why it works: memory is editable. When Muse gets you wrong, correcting it once fixes every future task that touches that fact.

templates.content:
# The Outcome-Prompt Wizard

Agents don't fail for lack of smarts — they fail on vague instructions. This wizard turns "hey, look into flights" into a brief a professional would sign off on. Paste the whole block into Muse and answer what it asks.

---

Copy-paste:

> Act as my briefing wizard. I have a rough task idea and I want you to turn it into a tight outcome-brief before doing any work. Interview me with these four sections, one at a time:
>
> **1. OUTCOME** — What does "done" look like in one sentence? Push me until it's concrete and measurable, not "look into" or "research."
>
> **2. DONE** — What exactly will you hand me at the end? (A shortlist? A booked ticket? A draft email?) Name the deliverable and its format.
>
> **3. BOUNDARIES** — What's off-limits? Use three lanes: RESEARCH (look freely, change nothing), DECIDE (bring me options, I pick), ACT (only with my explicit go-ahead — money, messages, bookings, commitments).
>
> **4. WHEN TO ASK** — What should make you stop and check with me instead of guessing? (Budget ceilings, dates I'm flexible on, people I won't contact.)
>
> When all four are answered, write the final brief back to me in under 150 words and wait for my go-ahead before starting.

---

## Why the BOUNDARIES step matters most

Muse's approval system is its superpower — but only if it knows where your lines are. "Research freely, never book" said once beats ten interrupted "should I proceed?" checkpoints. Most agent frustration is a boundaries problem wearing a prompt problem's clothes.

## Example: flight research

Rough idea: "find me a Denver flight."
After the wizard: "OUTCOME: three bookable CVG→DEN round-trips Nov 14–16 under $350, aisle preferred. DONE: comparison table with total prices. BOUNDARIES: research only — no booking, no account logins. WHEN TO ASK: if nothing is under $350, or if the only options are red-eyes."

Research that airline's delay-compensation policy and DOT rules, then draft me a firm but polite compensation request email citing the specific policy. Real result: a user got $250 out of a delay with this exact shape. Airlines bank on you not knowing the policy. Now you do.

## 2. Hold-and-call-back customer service

> I need to [cancel / dispute / renegotiate] with [COMPANY]. Research their retention/cancellation playbook: the best number to call, the magic words that get to a human or a supervisor, and what leverage I actually have (competitor offers, loyalty tenure). Give me a 5-bullet call script. I'll make the call; you do the intel.

> I'm traveling [DATES] to [PLACE] for [PURPOSE]. Weather looks like [X]. Build a packing list organized by day/outfit, plus a "buy before you go" list and a "don't forget" list of the things everyone forgets (chargers, meds, the thing for the thing). Keep it to one carry-on if possible.

templates.description: Twelve prompts are a lot; these are the four that matter. They don't generate content — they give you control over the agent: what it remembers, what it can touch, and what it knows about you. Run all four in your first week.
templates.content:
# The Power-User Checklist

Content prompts are fun. Control prompts are power. These four come from the community's complete-guide canon — run them once and you'll operate Muse like an owner, not a tourist.

## 1. Memory inspection

> Show me what you've learned about me so far — everything in your memory. Flag anything that's wrong, outdated, or that you'd be unsure about, and I'll correct it.

Run this monthly. Memory drift is real: old addresses, finished projects, changed preferences. A five-minute audit keeps every future answer sharper.

## 2. Permission-scope review

> Walk me through every permission and connector you've got on my account: what can read, what can write, and what asks first. For each write-level access, tell me in plain English the worst realistic thing that could happen if something went wrong.

This is the single highest-leverage safety prompt in the Muse canon. Most users grant access once and never look again. Don't be most users.

## 3. Business next step from your own records

> Look at my [calendar + email + notes from the last 30 days] and tell me: what's the single highest-leverage next step for [MY BUSINESS / MY JOB HUNT / MY PROJECT]? Not a list of ten — one thing, with your reasoning and what you'd need from me to start it.

Constraining it to ONE thing is the trick. Agents love lists; owners need priorities.

## 4. Training opt-out + data hygiene

> Walk me through checking whether my chats are used for training, and turn that off if it's on. Then tell me what data of mine you can see right now across all connected sources.

Your data, your call. Know the setting exists before you need it.

---

The meta-lesson: the users who get the most from Muse aren't the best prompt writers — they're the ones who've inspected the machine they're driving.

templates.content:
# Weekly Business Brief — Skill

This is a skill, not a prompt: paste the whole block and Muse executes the full method, not just one step.

---

Copy-paste:

> Run my Weekly Business Brief. Here's the method — follow it exactly:
>
> **STEP 1 — Gather.** Pull the last 7 days from my [email, calendar, sales dashboard, ad accounts — connect what's relevant]. Note: revenue in, notable expenses out, pipeline movement, anything scheduled next week that needs prep.
>
> **STEP 2 — Score the week.** Give the week a 1–10 and one sentence on why. Then: the single best thing that happened, the single worst, and the most surprising.
>
> **STEP 3 — Risks.** What's quietly going wrong? Stale deals, rising costs, a key person going quiet, a campaign decaying. Name up to 3, with evidence.
>
> **STEP 4 — Next week's three moves.** Not ten — three. Each with: the move, why it's the leverage point, what you need from me to start, and what "done" looks like.
>
> **STEP 5 — The brief.** Deliver it all as a tight brief under 500 words, numbers first, opinions clearly labeled as opinions. Save it as an artifact I can revisit.

---

## Make it recurring

Once the first brief lands and you like the shape, say: "Run this every Monday at 7am." That's the whole upgrade — one great skill, on a schedule, becomes an operating system.

## Customize the inputs

Swap the sources in Step 1 for your stack: Shopify instead of a dashboard, HubSpot instead of a spreadsheet, Stripe instead of invoices. The method doesn't care where the numbers live.

templates.content:
# Competitor Research Dive — Skill

Paste the block, name the competitor, get a teardown. The skill does the whole job: research, structure, and the "so what."

---

Copy-paste:

> Run a Competitor Research Dive on [COMPANY / PRODUCT]. Follow this method exactly:
>
> **STEP 1 — Snapshot.** What do they sell, to whom, at what price? One paragraph. Then their positioning in one sentence — what they'd say makes them different.
>
> **STEP 2 — Evidence.** Find: their pricing page details, 3 recent launches or announcements, what their customers praise AND complain about (reviews, Reddit, social — quote real voices), and who's talking about them this month.
>
> **STEP 3 — Content & channels.** Where do they show up? (Blog, YouTube, X, podcasts, ads.) What's their cadence, and which 2-3 pieces actually performed? What are they NOT doing that their audience wants?
>
> **STEP 4 — My openings.** Based on all of the above: three gaps I could exploit — each with why it's real (evidence, not vibes), how hard it'd be, and the first concrete step.
>
> **STEP 5 — Deliverable.** A brief under 600 words plus a one-page comparison table: them vs. me on price, positioning, content, and momentum. Save as an artifact.

---

## Rules that keep it honest

- Quote real customers; never invent testimonials or metrics. If you can't verify a number, say so.
- Recency matters: weight the last 90 days heaviest. A 2024 pricing page is archaeology.
- Openings must trace to evidence from Steps 1–3. "They're weak on video" needs a finding, not a feeling.

## Job-hunter variant

Replace [COMPANY] with your target employer and add to Step 4: "three things I should mention in the interview to show I did my homework." Hiring managers notice.

templates.title: Anatomy of a Great SKILL.md
templates.tagline: How Meta itself structures skills: scope discipline, evidence-matched claims, and rules an agent can actually follow.
templates.description: Not a drop-in skill — a pattern reference. Distilled from the structure of Meta's own in-house skills: the operating rules that make a skill reliable instead of decorative. Use it as the skeleton every time you write your own SKILL.md.
templates.content:
# Anatomy of a Great SKILL.md

The best skills read like an operator's handbook, not a feature list. This pattern is distilled from how Meta structures its own agent skills. Steal the skeleton; write your own muscle.

## The skeleton

```markdown
# [Skill name] — what it does in one line

## When to use
[The trigger conditions. Be specific: "when the user asks about ad performance" beats "for marketing tasks."]

## Scope — what this skill touches
- READS: [exact sources — never "everything" or "relevant data"]
- WRITES: [exact destinations, or "nothing — read-only"]
- NEVER: [the bright lines — money movement, external sends, credential storage]

## Method
[Numbered steps the agent follows in order. Each step names its input, its action, and its output. If a step needs a judgment call, say who makes it.]

## Evidence rules
- Every number gets a source. No source, no number — say "unverified" instead.
- Progress claims match what actually happened: "drafted" ≠ "sent", "researched" ≠ "decided".
- Never write tool observations into memory as facts. Observations are transient; memory is durable.

## Output contract
[Exactly what the user receives: format, length cap, where it's saved. "A brief under 400 words, saved as an artifact" beats "a summary."]

## Failure modes
[What to do when the skill can't complete: which step to stop at, what to tell the user, what never to fake.]
```

## Why each section earns its place

- **When to use** stops the skill firing on the wrong tasks — the #1 skill bug.
- **Scope** is the safety system: explicit read/write/never lists mean the agent doesn't improvise permissions.
- **Method** turns a vibe into a procedure. Numbered, ordered, with named inputs and outputs.
- **Evidence rules** are what separate a professional skill from a confident liar. "Drafted ≠ sent" alone prevents an entire class of disasters.
- **Output contract** kills the "here's a 2,000-word essay when you wanted a checklist" problem.
- **Failure modes** are the mark of a skill that's been run in the real world. Write them after your first three runs, not before your first.

## The one-line test

Show your SKILL.md to someone who's never met your agent. If they can predict what it will do — and what it will refuse to do — it's ready. If they can't, the scope section is lying.

templates.title: The First Four Automations
templates.tagline: The definitive onboarding order: morning briefing, email triage, goal tracking, Friday review. Don't automate #4 before #1.
templates.description: The community's highest-value automation sequence: four scheduled tasks in the order that earns trust. Start with the morning briefing (highest value per minute of setup), earn confidence, then expand. Describe outcomes, not procedures — Muse figures out the how.
templates.content:
# The First Four Automations

New Muse users automate the wrong thing first — usually something complex, which fails, which teaches them "automation doesn't work." The community's hard-won onboarding order fixes that: each automation earns the trust the next one needs.

## Automation 1 — Morning briefing (week 1)

> Every weekday at 7:00 AM, brief me: calendar today with one-line prep per meeting, top 3 overnight items in [MY INDUSTRY], and anything urgent in my inbox I haven't seen. Under 300 words. Push it to me.

Why first: highest value per minute of setup. You'll feel it on day one, which is the whole point — early wins fund later ambition.

## Automation 2 — Email triage (week 2)

> Twice daily (8 AM, 4 PM), triage my inbox: what's urgent, what can wait, what needs a reply from me vs. what you can draft. Draft the replies; never send. Flag anything from [KEY PEOPLE] immediately regardless of time.

Why second: you already trust the briefing. Triage is the same muscle with higher stakes — and the "draft, never send" guardrail keeps it safe while you calibrate.

## Automation 3 — Goal tracking (week 3)

> Every evening at 9 PM, check me against [MY GOAL — e.g. "ship the launch", "run 3x this week", "inbox zero Fridays"]: what moved today, what's blocked, and the single most important thing for tomorrow. Keep a running score I can review.

Why third: now Muse has context (your calendar, your inbox) and you have trust. Goals turn the agent from reactive to proactive.

## Automation 4 — Friday review (week 4)

> Every Friday at 4 PM: this week's wins, misses, and open loops across my calendar, email, and goals. Then propose next week's top 3 priorities and wait for my edit before finalizing.

Why last: the review synthesizes everything before it. Run it in week one and it's generic; run it in week four and it's personal.

---

## The standing rule

Describe OUTCOMES, not procedures. "Brief me on my day" beats "check my calendar API, then my email API, then format as bullets." Muse is an agent — let it agent. Your job is the what and the boundaries; its job is the how.
