templates.title: Family Schedule Watchdog
templates.tagline: 4 kids, 4 sports, 4 messaging apps — one daily digest. The best non-technical Muse win in the canon.
templates.description: The community's favorite non-technical win: a parent with schedules scattered across four messaging apps gets one daily push digest of everyone's day. No coding, no dashboards — just the chaos, tamed.
templates.content:
# Family Schedule Watchdog

The setup, as posted: four kids, four sports, schedules living in four different messaging apps. One parent, zero spare attention. Muse fixed it with a single scheduled task — and the parent self-describes as non-technical. If they can run this, you can.

## The recipe

Copy-paste, filling the brackets:

> You are my family operations chief. Here's where our schedules live: [list the sources — group chats, school apps, team apps, calendar].
>
> Every weekday at [6:30 AM], send me one digest:
> - **Today per person:** [KID 1]: [what/where/time], [KID 2]: ..., including who's driving whom
> - **Conflicts:** anything double-booked, overlapping pickups, or missing drivers — flagged FIRST, before the schedule
> - **Prep:** anything we need to pack/bring/pay today, with deadlines
> - **Tomorrow preview:** one line per person so nothing ambushes us
>
> Rules: if a schedule changes mid-day in any source, alert me immediately — don't wait for the morning digest. When in doubt about who's driving, ask; never guess on logistics involving kids.

## Why it works

- **One source of truth.** The digest IS the schedule. Stop checking four apps.
- **Conflicts first.** The most valuable line in the digest is the one that prevents the 5 PM panic.
- **Change alerts.** Morning digests go stale by noon; the mid-day change rule is what makes it a watchdog instead of a newsletter.

## Level-ups (month two)

- Sunday evening: full-week preview with the week's conflict map.
- Shared version: a second digest formatted for your partner / co-parent.
- Season rollover: "new season starting — re-scan all sources and rebuild the roster."

templates.title: The Goal-Artifact Loop
templates.tagline: Turn any goal into a tracked artifact with follow-ups: the signature Muse workflow shape.
templates.description: Muse's signature move: a goal becomes a living artifact, and the artifact drives ongoing follow-up. Distilled from a community reviewer's 24-week marathon build and photo meal-logging setup. The pattern works for any goal with a timeline.
templates.content:
# The Goal-Artifact Loop

The most Muse-native workflow in the canon: you don't get advice, you get an artifact — a living document the agent keeps updating as you report in. Here's the loop, ready to run on your goal.

## The setup prompt

> I want to [GOAL — e.g. "run a marathon in 24 weeks", "ship my product by March", "learn Spanish to conversational"]. Build me a tracked plan as an artifact:
>
> **The plan:** break it into phases with milestones I can actually hit. Be honest about what's hard — flag anything I should check with a professional first (doctor, coach, accountant — name the right one, don't play one).
>
> **The loop:** check in with me [daily/weekly] — ask what I did, log it against the plan, and adjust the coming weeks based on reality, not the fantasy schedule. If I miss twice in a row, ask what's actually wrong instead of just rescheduling.
>
> **The artifact:** keep one living document — current phase, progress log, upcoming milestones, and your honest assessment of whether I'm on track. Update it every check-in.

## Why the loop beats the plan

Plans die on contact with real life. The loop survives because it has a repair mechanism: the "missed twice" rule forces a real conversation instead of silent drift. Most goal systems track; this one notices.

## The meal-logging variant

Same loop, smaller cycle:

> I'm logging my meals by photo. When I send one, identify what you see, ask me about anything unclear (portions, hidden ingredients), log it, and at day's end give me an honest read — not a lecture, a read. Keep a running weekly summary in the artifact.

Photo in, judgment-free log out, weekly pattern visible. The artifact is what turns 200 meal photos into actual insight.

## Rules for the human

- Report honestly. The loop is only as good as your check-ins — "I skipped" beats silence.
- Let it adjust the plan. A plan that can't change is a guilt machine.
- Keep the professional-flag rule: the agent advises, experts clear.

templates.title: Email Marketing Audit
templates.tagline: Connect Klaviyo + Shopify, find the duplicate flows bleeding revenue, approve every fix. A real founder's cleanup.
templates.description: A concrete business automation with a named real-world win: a founder's duplicate-flow cleanup via Klaviyo + Shopify. The workflow audits your active flows, flags misconfigurations, drafts fixes for your approval, and keeps watching.
templates.content:
# Email Marketing Audit — Workflow

A real founder ran this and found duplicate flows quietly bleeding revenue. The workflow is read-first, fix-second, monitor-always — and nothing publishes without your approval.

## The audit prompt

> Audit my email marketing. I use [Klaviyo / Mailchimp / etc.] connected to [Shopify / WooCommerce / etc.].
>
> **STEP 1 — Map.** List every active flow: name, trigger, audience, and what it sends. Build me the full inventory — I probably don't know everything that's live.
>
> **STEP 2 — Diagnose.** Flag: duplicate triggers (two flows firing on the same event), missing tracking (flows that can't prove revenue), dead segments (audiences that never get mailed), and timing collisions (three emails landing the same day).
>
> **STEP 3 — Draft fixes.** For each issue: what you'd change, why, and the expected effect. Draft the actual fix (new trigger logic, suppressed segment, rewritten subject line) but change NOTHING yet.
>
> **STEP 4 — Approval.** Present the fixes ranked by revenue impact. I approve each one individually before you touch anything.
>
> **STEP 5 — Monitor.** After fixes go live, watch for anomalies weekly: sudden drop in flow revenue, unsubscribe spikes, deliverability dips. Alert me with the data, not a vibe.

## What the founder found

Duplicate flows on the same trigger — the classic. Two "abandoned cart" sequences both live, both firing, customers getting doubled up. The audit caught it in step 2; the fix was a ten-minute suppression rule. That's the whole pitch: the money was already being lost, quietly, every day.

## The discipline that makes it safe

Steps 3 and 4 are separated on purpose. Drafting is cheap; publishing is not. An agent that drafts brilliantly and publishes recklessly is a liability — the approval gate between them is the entire safety model.

templates.title: Read-Only-First Rollout
templates.tagline: The safety doctrine: summarize → draft → send → revoke. Standing files, vault hygiene, approval discipline.
templates.description: The safety doctrine every Vault template assumes: a four-rung rollout ladder (summarize, draft, send, revoke), standing files that persist your rules, and credential hygiene. From the community practitioner's guide to delegating safely.
templates.content:
# Read-Only-First Rollout

The core insight: you don't grant an agent power and hope. You climb a ladder — each rung earned by the last one working. Four rungs, in order, no skipping.

## The ladder

**Rung 1 — SUMMARIZE (read-only).** The agent reads and reports. Nothing changes, nothing sends, nothing drafts. Run here for a week.

> "For the next 7 days: read-only. Summarize my inbox, my calendar, my docs — change nothing, draft nothing. I want to see what you notice before I let you touch anything."

**Rung 2 — DRAFT (write, don't send).** The agent prepares; you execute. Drafts, plans, comparisons — all waiting for your hand on the button.

> "You may now draft replies, plans, and documents. Nothing sends, books, buys, or publishes without my explicit approval on each item."

**Rung 3 — SEND (bounded action).** Specific, named permissions — one lane at a time. "You may send the Tuesday newsletter draft after I approve it" is a rung-3 grant. "Handle my email" is not.

**Rung 4 — REVOKE (prove you can take it back).** The forgotten rung. Once a quarter, revoke something and confirm the agent actually stops. A permission you can't revoke was never really yours.

## Standing files — your rules, persisted

The guide's second doctrine: don't re-explain yourself every chat. Keep standing files the agent reads every session:

- **What to remember:** durable facts (timezone, airport, budget lines, communication style)
- **How to act:** your boundaries (the three lanes: research freely / bring me options / act only on approval)
- **How to talk:** terse vs. thorough, when to ask vs. decide

Tell Muse once: "Save this to your memory / standing instructions." Then correct it when it drifts — memory is editable, and the corrections compound.

## Credential hygiene

The agent should NEVER ask for your raw passwords. The correct flow: the service's official sign-in (OAuth, "Sign in with Google"), or a secure vault handoff — never a password pasted into chat. If an agent asks for a password in chat, that's a red flag about the agent, not a normal step.

templates.title: The Safe Setup Checklist
templates.tagline: 13 real-world tests distilled: the 5-step safe setup and what to delegate vs. what to verify.
templates.description: What 13 real-world delegation tests actually taught: a 5-step safe setup (name the agent, calendar first, read-only email, training opt-out, staged purchase approval) plus trust verdicts — what to delegate freely and what to always verify.
templates.content:
# The Safe Setup Checklist

Thirteen real-world tests. One clear pattern: Muse is excellent at research and drafting, dangerous at unsupervised action, and the difference is entirely in your setup. Do these five steps before you delegate anything real.

## The 5-step safe setup

**1. Name your agent.** Give it a name and a role in its first message. ("You're my ops chief.") Named agents get treated — by you and by the agent — as accountable. Unnamed ones get vague instructions.

**2. Calendar first.** Connect the calendar before anything else. It's read-mostly, high-value, and it teaches you the approval rhythm on safe ground.

**3. Read-only email.** Connect email as READ-ONLY first. Let it summarize and triage for a week before it ever drafts — and drafts before it ever sends. (See: the read-only-first ladder.)

**4. Training opt-out.** Check whether your chats train the model; turn it off if you want. Know where your words go before you put real business in them.

**5. Purchase approval, staged.** First purchase-adjacent task: "research only." Second: "draft the order, I'll click buy." Third+: bounded approval with a dollar ceiling. Never jump from zero to "just handle it."

## What to delegate vs. what to verify

From the 13 tests, the trust map:

**Delegate freely:** research briefs, comparisons, drafting, scheduling, summaries, monitoring/alerting, data organization.

**Always verify:** anything with money moving, anything sent in your name, anything published, any fact you'll repeat publicly, any permission change.

**The rule of thumb:** if undo is one click, delegate. If undo is a phone call, verify. If undo is impossible, do it yourself.

## The calibration habit

After each delegated task, ask: "What did you get wrong or guess at?" Agents that report their own uncertainty are agents you can trust further. Agents that never admit a guess are agents you watch closer.

templates.title: Muse Under the Hood (Unofficial)
templates.tagline: The community-reconstructed agent reference: skills catalog, artifact tools, standing files, runtime model.
templates.description: UNOFFICIAL — a community reconstruction of Muse's agent internals, not Meta documentation. The definitive under-the-hood reference for power users writing their own system prompts and skills: the skills catalog shape, artifact tools, standing files, and how background tasks deliver.
templates.content:
# Muse Under the Hood — UNOFFICIAL Community Reference

> **Provenance warning:** this is a community reconstruction assembled from public sources — NOT official Meta documentation. Treat it as a map drawn by explorers, not the territory. Useful for understanding the shape of the machine; not gospel about any specific version.

## The architecture, as the community understands it

**The agent loop.** Muse runs a loop: understand the request → plan → use tools (with your approval at the checkpoints you set) → report back. Everything it does fits in that loop. When it seems stuck, it's usually a planning problem (vague goal) or a permission problem (missing grant) — not a smarts problem.

**Skills catalog.** Skills are reusable methods the agent can invoke — each with a name, a trigger ("when to use"), and a procedure. Think of them as apps the agent installs on demand. The community writes them as SKILL.md files: scope, method, evidence rules, output contract.

**Artifact tools.** When output deserves to persist — a document, a sheet, a page, audio — the agent builds an artifact instead of a chat reply. Rule of thumb the community converged on: if you'll revisit it, artifact it; if it's fire-and-forget, chat is fine.

**Standing files.** The agent carries persistent context across sessions: who you are, what you've decided, what's in memory, how you like to work. This is why "feed its memory" (see: Five Prompts That Get Better Answers) is the highest-leverage beginner move — you're programming the standing layer.

**Memory vs. conversation.** Conversation is short-term: what you're talking about now. Memory is long-term: what the agent should know next month. Corrections to memory ("you remembered X wrong") compound across every future session.

**Background tasks.** Scheduled tasks and crons run the agent loop on a timer — briefings, triage, monitoring — and deliver results as notifications or artifacts. The Vault's "Crons & Automations" category is this layer, productized.

**Approvals as checkpoints.** Money, messages, filings, publishes — the agent stops and asks. This isn't friction; it's the control plane. Your standing files should define the lanes (research freely / bring options / act on approval) so checkpoints fire only where they matter.

## How to use this reference

- **Writing system prompts:** mirror the shape — role, scope, method, evidence rules, output contract. (See: Anatomy of a Great SKILL.md.)
- **Debugging weird behavior:** check which layer failed — goal vague? permission missing? memory stale? — instead of blaming "the AI."
- **Setting expectations:** the community's trust map (see: Safe Setup Checklist) is the practical companion to this reference.

## What NOT to do with this

Don't quote it as Meta policy. Don't build security assumptions on it. Don't assume any version number. It's a community map — good for orientation, not for navigation in the dark.

templates.title: Connector Permissions, Decoded
templates.tagline: Allow / Ask / Deny: the anatomy every Muse user gets wrong, plus the secrets hygiene that keeps you safe.
templates.description: The #1 thing Muse users get wrong: connector permissions. Every connector splits into read and write actions; 'Ask' is the sweet spot; defaults aren't your settings. Plus the secrets rule: the agent never needs your raw password.
templates.content:
# Connector Permissions, Decoded

Every connector — Gmail, Calendar, Shopify, all of them — splits into individual read and write actions. Most users click through once and never look again. This is the guide to looking again.

## Allow / Ask / Deny — what they actually mean

- **ALLOW:** the agent uses this action freely, no checkpoint. Right for: reading your calendar, searching email, fetching data. Wrong for: sending email, moving money, publishing anything.
- **ASK:** the agent stops and asks each time. This is the sweet spot for most write actions — sending a draft, creating a calendar event, placing an order. Slight friction, total control.
- **DENY:** the action is off entirely. Use for: anything you never want the agent touching (deleting emails, refunding orders, posting publicly).

## The audit (15 minutes, quarterly)

> "Walk me through every connector on my account. For each one: list every action set to ALLOW, and for each write-level ALLOW, tell me the worst realistic outcome if the agent used it badly. Then recommend what I should switch to ASK or DENY, and why."

Run it. The answer is always surprising — there's always one ALLOW you forgot about.

## Defaults aren't your settings

Fresh connectors often default to the permissive side (it makes demos smooth). Your actual settings are whatever you set after the demo. The tutorial's mantra: "defaults aren't your settings." The first thing you do with any new connector is the audit above.

## Secrets hygiene — the bright line

- The agent NEVER needs your raw password. Real connections use the service's official sign-in (OAuth / "Sign in with Google") or a secure vault handoff.
- If any agent, skill, or prompt asks you to paste a password or API key into chat: stop. That's not a normal step — it's either a scam or a badly built skill.
- API keys live in secure storage, referenced by name, never pasted into conversation.

## The three permission personas

- **The Researcher:** everything read-only, all writes DENY. For brand-new agents and untrusted skills.
- **The Drafter:** reads ALLOW, writes ASK. The default you should live in.
- **The Operator:** narrow, named ALLOWs ("may send the Tuesday newsletter after my approval"), everything else ASK. Earned over time, reviewed quarterly.

Start as the Researcher. Graduate to Drafter. Promote to Operator one lane at a time.

templates.title: The Bounded Delegation Checklist
templates.tagline: Define → grant → review → audit: the canonical checklist before any money-adjacent task.
templates.description: The canonical safe-delegation checklist: define a bounded task, grant only the access it needs, review every proposed action before it fires, audit the trail after. Run it before any task involving money, messages, or commitments.
templates.content:
# The Bounded Delegation Checklist

Before you hand Muse anything involving money, messages, or commitments, run this four-step checklist. It takes five minutes and prevents the entire category of "the agent did WHAT?" stories.

## Step 1 — DEFINE the bounded task

Write the task as a contract:

> Task: [one sentence]. Success looks like: [observable outcome]. Out of scope: [what it must NOT touch]. Done means: [the deliverable you'll receive].

If you can't write the "out of scope" line, the task isn't bounded yet. Fix that first.

## Step 2 — GRANT only what's needed

Least privilege, literally:

> "For this task you may READ [exact sources]. You may WRITE [exact destinations, or 'nothing']. You may NOT [money movement / external sends / new permissions / anything else]. These grants expire when the task is done."

Name the sources. "Relevant data" is not a grant — it's a loophole.

## Step 3 — REVIEW every proposed action

Before anything fires, Muse should show you the action card:

- **What:** the exact action (send / pay / book / publish)
- **To whom / how much / where:** recipient, amount, destination — the concrete values, not descriptions
- **Undo:** how to reverse it if it's wrong

Your review checklist: right recipient? right amount? right timing? anything in the "out of scope" line? One "no" anywhere = stop and redefine.

## Step 4 — AUDIT the trail

After the task:

> "Show me everything you did: every action taken, every message sent, every dollar moved, with timestamps. Flag anything that deviated from the task contract."

Read the trail. The audit isn't distrust — it's how the next delegation gets a wider boundary. Clean trails earn trust; trust earns autonomy.

## The capability map (know what you're granting)

Muse's powers, roughly: conversation + memory, connected services (read/write per your grants), scheduled tasks, artifact building, web research, and approvals-as-checkpoints. When you grant access, you're granting slices of these — so grant slices, not the whole pie.

## The one-sentence version

"Tight task, tiny permissions, my eyes on every action, receipts afterwards."

Tape it to the wall.

templates.title: The Unclaimed Money Sweep
templates.tagline: Point Muse at state unclaimed-property databases, get a report on money owed to you — re-checked on a schedule.
templates.description: One prompt turned into $1,500 found across two states. Every US state holds forgotten money — old deposits, refunds, paychecks — and searching it is public-record legwork, exactly what an agent is for. This template gives you the verbatim prompt from the thread plus the setup that makes the recurring check actually work.
templates.content:
# The Unclaimed Money Sweep

A Reddit user asked Muse to look for money owed to them. It found over **$1,500 in unclaimed funds across two states** they'd lived in — then kept checking every 5 days and reporting back. The whole thing is one prompt plus a schedule.

## The prompt (verbatim from the thread)

> Can you look around the internet for any money that might be owed to me? Please check my claim status every 5 days and report back to me on any changes.

## Make it work better than the bare prompt

**Give it your name variants.** Unclaimed-property records are literal. Tell Muse every version of your name to search: maiden/married names, middle initial vs. full middle name, common misspellings.

**Give it your states.** List every state you've lived or worked in, with rough years. That's the search surface — one state at a time misses the money.

> Search unclaimed-property records for [NAME VARIANTS] in [STATES, with years]. Report every match with the holder, amount, and claim link. Do not file any claims — report only, I'll file them myself.

**Keep it read-only.** Filing a claim requires identity verification and personal documents. That's your job. Muse's job is the search and the watch. Say so explicitly and it won't try to submit anything in your name.

## The recurring check

The 5-day re-check is the part most people skip. New unclaimed funds get posted constantly — a one-time search goes stale. Set it as a scheduled Muse task: "check for new matches every [5 days / weekly], report only if something changed."

## What to expect

Most people find nothing or small amounts. Some find real money — the thread's $1,500 came from two forgotten accounts in old states of residence. The search costs you one prompt. The expected value is wildly asymmetric.

templates.title: Stealth DM Screen
templates.tagline: Have Muse screen your unread Instagram DMs and report back — without flipping anything to read.
templates.description: The notification-shade trick, automated. A Reddit user had Muse screen 50 unread Instagram threads: it peeked at the ones they named, reported what people sent, and the unread count stayed at 50 — nothing flipped to read on either end. For the message you can't ignore but don't want to open yet.
templates.content:
# Stealth DM Screen

You know the trick where you read a DM from the notification shade so it never shows as read? A Reddit user found Muse does that for your Instagram DMs — except it can read all of them.

Their words: they asked Muse to screen unread threads one morning. It came back with 50 unread, peeked at the ones they named, and told them what people sent. **Unread count was still 50 afterward. Nothing flipped to read — not on their end, not on the sender's.**

## Setup (one time)

1. In Muse settings, add **Instagram** and **Instagram Messages** as connectors, then log in.
2. That's the whole setup.

## The ask

> Screen my unread Instagram DMs. Tell me how many are unread, then for the threads I name, tell me what each person sent — without marking anything as read.

If you have a creator or professional account, Instagram splits DMs into folders — **Primary, General, message requests** — and Muse can pull from any of them. Name the folder when you ask.

## When this earns its keep

- **The message you don't want to engage with yet** — but there's a detail in the history you need. Peek, retrieve, stay unread.
- **Morning triage** — "summarize everything unread from overnight, flag anything urgent" beats opening 50 threads.
- **Message requests** — screen the stranger folder without signaling you've seen anything.

## The boundary

This is read-only by design. Muse reports; it doesn't reply, doesn't react, doesn't open threads in your app. If you want it to draft a reply to something it screened, that's a separate ask with your explicit go-ahead — the screen itself never sends anything.

templates.title: The Self-Improving Skills Loop
templates.tagline: Mine your own chat history for repeated mistakes, then have Muse write the missing skills so they never repeat.
templates.description: Your Muse sessions are full of repeated friction — the same correction explained twice, the same job hand-run every week. This loop turns that waste into fuel: scan your history for the patterns, generate one missing skill per pattern, and let a scheduled daily-notes task keep the whole system compounding. One real-world case: 3.5 hours of weekly note-taking collapsed to 4 minutes. The before/after is measurable the day you start.
templates.content:
# The Self-Improving Skills Loop

Fixing an agent in chat is like shouting at a goldfish. It forgets. Writing the fix into a skill makes it permanent. This loop finds the fixes worth writing — automatically.

## Why it works

Every repeated mistake you correct in chat is a skill you haven't written yet. Your session history is the evidence. Mine it, generate the skill, schedule the loop. That's the whole system.

## Step 1 — Find your repeated friction

Open a fresh Muse session and paste this:

> Scan my recent session history for repeated patterns: jobs I ask for more than once, corrections I've had to explain twice or more, and formats I always have to re-specify. List each pattern with a count of how many times it occurred. Rank the list by frequency. Don't fix anything yet — just show me the evidence.

You now have a ranked hit list. The top item is your first skill.

## Step 2 — Turn one pattern into a skill

Paste this for the top pattern only:

> Create a personal skill for the job "[job name from your list]".
>
> Use the prompts I wrote for this job in my session history as the source. Include: the steps I always ask for, my format and length rules, my tone, and two good examples from my past sessions.
>
> Write the description so it triggers whenever I ask for this job, even if I phrase it differently.
>
> Save it to ~/.claude/skills/[skillname]/SKILL.md and show me the file.

Rules that keep it honest:

- **One skill at a time.** Use it for a full week before building the next.
- **Test the trigger.** Ask for the job the lazy way, in a fresh session. If Muse doesn't pick up the skill, the description is too narrow. If it fires on the wrong jobs, too broad.
- **Description is the skill.** That's how Muse decides when to load it. Specific beats clever.

## Step 3 — Close the loop with a scheduled daily-notes task

The pattern compounds when it's automatic. Set up a scheduled task that runs every morning:

> Every morning at 9:00 AM, generate my daily work notes: pull what I worked on yesterday from my session history, list what I finished, what's still open, and anything I'm repeating that should become a skill. Keep it under 200 words.

Now your agent does three things daily: report, track, and nominate the next skill. The friction list maintains itself.

## Step 4 — The honest metrics

This works if you measure it:

- **Before:** count the weekly minutes you spend on the job. Time it once.
- **After 2 weeks:** time it again. If the number didn't move, the skill's description or steps are wrong — rewrite the file, not the chat.
- **The benchmark that went viral:** 3.5 hours/week of manual daily notes down to 4 minutes. Your numbers will be smaller. Smaller still counts.

## What to avoid

- **Don't build the second skill before testing the first.** An untested skill is just a file you forgot about.
- **Don't fix in chat what belongs in the skill.** When a mistake repeats, the bug is in SKILL.md, not in this conversation.
- **Don't mine history for one-off jobs.** Skills are for recurring work. One-offs stay in chat.

## Pair it with

- *Anatomy of a Great SKILL.md* — the skeleton to write inside once you've found the pattern.
- The "gate" rule: each skill needs a definition of done and one perfect example, or the agent scores itself against nothing.

templates.title: The Claim Check
templates.tagline: Paste any claim, get a verdict with receipts — evidence ranked, conflicts flagged, confidence stated.
templates.description: The most-used Grok move on X is the instant fact-check: tag the bot, ask 'is this true,' get an answer. Hundreds of thousands of people do it — and the bare version is where they get burned, because a confident verdict with no receipts is just an opinion with better posture. This template keeps the one-paste speed and adds the discipline: the claim gets decomposed, evidence gets ranked by source quality, disagreements between sources get surfaced instead of smoothed over, and the verdict ends with what would change it.
templates.content:
# The Claim Check

On X, the reflex is "@grok is this true?" — researchers counted over 447,000 fact-check requests in seven months. The reflex is right. The execution is the problem: a bare yes/no from any model is a coin flip wearing a suit.

This is the same move with a spine. One paste, structured verdict, receipts attached.

## The prompt

Paste this, then paste the claim:

> Run a claim check on what follows. Work in this exact order:
>
> 1. **Restate the claim** in one sentence, exactly as it's being asserted — no softening, no strengthening.
> 2. **Split it** into its checkable parts. Most viral claims are three claims in a trench coat. List each part separately.
> 3. **Check each part** against the best sources you can reach. Rank evidence by this ladder: primary documents and official records first, then established reporting, then expert commentary, then social posts. A claim sourced only from posts repeating each other is unverified, not confirmed.
> 4. **Verdict per part:** Supported / Contradicted / Contested / Unverifiable — with the strongest single piece of evidence for the verdict and a link or citation for it.
> 5. **Conflicts:** if credible sources disagree, say so plainly and show both. Never average a disagreement into a mushy middle.
> 6. **Confidence:** High / Medium / Low per part, and one line on what evidence would change the verdict.
>
> End with a one-line overall verdict. Do not open with caveats; open with the verdict.

## Why the structure matters

- **Decomposition is the whole game.** "The city banned X and crime doubled" is two claims with different evidence. Checking them as one produces one wrong answer instead of two right ones.
- **The ladder stops circular sourcing.** Fifty posts citing one unsourced post is one source, not fifty.
- **"What would change this" keeps it honest.** A verdict that can't name its flip condition is a belief, not a check.

## Use it on

Screenshots of headlines, forwarded statistics, "did you hear" claims in group chats, a competitor's marketing claim, a quote attributed to someone famous, your own draft before you publish a number in it.

## The boundary

A claim check is a first pass, not a citation. For anything you're going to publish, sign, or spend money on, open the primary source it points you to. The template's job is to get you to the right document fast — and to tell you plainly when the document doesn't exist.

templates.title: One-Source Deep Research
templates.tagline: Restrict the research to one firehose — a platform, a forum, your reviews — and mine it completely instead of skimming the whole web.
templates.description: The sharpest Grok research pattern going around operator circles flips normal research on its head: instead of searching everywhere, you forbid everywhere. One builder's market-research system runs DeepSearch against X posts only — no websites, no blogs — and extracts competitor complaints, feature requests, and pain points in customers' actual words, then builds market segments out of them. The constraint is the quality: a single source read completely beats the whole internet skimmed. This template generalizes the move to any bounded corpus you can point Muse at.
templates.content:
# One-Source Deep Research

Most AI research fails the same way: the model skims forty sources and returns the average of the internet. The Grok pattern that operators keep sharing does the opposite — it **restricts the universe to one source and reads it completely.**

The original: a market-research system that searches X posts *only* — explicitly no other websites — to learn what customers complain about, request, and compare. Blogs tell you what companies say. The firehose tells you what buyers say.

## The prompt

> Research [TOPIC / MARKET / PRODUCT] using ONLY this source universe: [ONE SOURCE — e.g. "posts in this subreddit," "the reviews pasted below," "this platform's posts from the last 90 days," "these support tickets"]. Do not use any other source, and say so if the universe is too thin to answer.
>
> Extract, in the source's own language (paraphrase closely, don't sanitize):
>
> 1. **The players:** every competitor or alternative mentioned, with what people say it's for.
> 2. **Complaints:** recurring criticisms, each with a rough count of how often it appears. A complaint mentioned once is an anecdote; five times is a signal.
> 3. **Requests:** features, fixes, and "I wish it did X" statements, counted the same way.
> 4. **Switching stories:** any "I moved from A to B because…" accounts, quoted closely — these are the highest-value items in the set.
> 5. **Segments:** group the voices into 4–6 distinct camps by what they're trying to get done, and name each camp by its job, not its demographics.
>
> End with: the three findings a competitor would least want public, and the thinnest part of the evidence — where the universe didn't have enough signal.

## Picking your universe

- **A platform's posts** (a subreddit, a forum, X search results you've pulled): best for market and competitor research.
- **Your own reviews / tickets / survey verbatims:** best for product decisions — the complaints are already about you.
- **One publication or doc set:** best for "what does this source actually claim across everything it's published."

Feed Muse the corpus directly (paste, attach, or connect it) whenever you can. A universe it can actually read beats a universe it has to imagine.

## Rules that keep it true

- **Counts or it didn't happen.** Every pattern needs a frequency, or it's one loud voice impersonating a market.
- **Paraphrase closely.** The value is in the customers' framing, not the model's summary of it.
- **Thin is a finding.** If the universe can't answer, the correct output is "not enough signal" — and that tells you where to look next.

templates.title: The 48-Hour Brief
templates.tagline: Everything published on a topic in the last 48 hours — ranked by credibility, conflicts shown, unknowns admitted.
templates.description: The Grok prompt shape that gets shared more than any other research format: compile everything from the last 48 hours on a topic, rank the sources by credibility, and highlight the conflicting claims. It exists because breaking topics are where AI answers quietly rot — the model's memory of a story is the version from before the update, the correction, the reversal. This template hard-codes the three things that make a fast brief trustworthy: a hard time window, a credibility ranking you can see, and a conflicts section that refuses to pretend the sources agree.
templates.content:
# The 48-Hour Brief

Something just happened in your market — a launch, an outage, a policy change, a competitor's move — and you need the current state of it, not the state of it as of some training cutoff. This is the brief format that Grok users converged on, rebuilt for Muse.

## The prompt

> Brief me on [TOPIC]. Rules:
>
> - **Window:** only material published in the last 48 hours counts as news. Anything older may be used as background, but label it BACKGROUND and date it.
> - **Timeline first:** a chronological list of what happened, each entry with its publication time and source. Newest understanding last.
> - **Credibility ranking:** rank sources in three tiers — primary (official statements, filings, the company/person directly), established reporting, and social/secondary. When tiers disagree, the higher tier wins and the disagreement gets noted.
> - **Conflicts section:** list every point where credible sources contradict each other — numbers, timelines, causes, quotes. Show both versions with their sources. Do not resolve a conflict by averaging it.
> - **What we don't know:** end with the open questions — the facts no source in the window has established yet.
>
> Keep the brief under 600 words. Every factual claim gets a source and a timestamp, or it doesn't go in.

## Variations that earn their keep

- **The launch brief:** same prompt, window stretched to 7 days, add a section: "Reaction — what practitioners (not commentators) are saying now that they've touched it."
- **The incident brief:** window at 24 hours, add: "What the responsible party has officially said, verbatim-summarized, separated from what others claim they said."
- **The standing brief:** turn it into a scheduled task — same prompt, run each morning, and instruct: "If nothing material changed since yesterday's brief, say exactly that in one line."

## Why the conflicts section is non-negotiable

Early coverage is wrong in predictable ways: the first number is a guess, the first cause is a rumor, the first quote is out of context. A brief that hides disagreement manufactures certainty you don't have. The conflicts list *is* the brief — it tells you what to wait on before you act.

## The honesty rule

If the window is empty — nothing credible published in 48 hours — the correct brief is one sentence saying so. A model that pads a quiet window with old news and speculation has failed the assignment, and this prompt tells it so up front.

templates.title: Debate Yourself
templates.tagline: Make Muse argue your decision from both sides — Advocate, Critic, Arbiter — and rule on which case is stronger, and why.
templates.description: The Grok technique every Heavy/Think-mode breakdown lands on: don't ask for an opinion, stage a debate. 'What are the arguments for and against this decision? Then tell me which is stronger and why.' It works because a single-pass answer defends whatever it said first, while a debate forces the strongest version of the other side into the room. This template formalizes it with three named roles, one rule for the Critic (attack the strongest points, never strawmen), and an Arbiter who is forbidden from calling a tie — and must name the evidence that would flip the ruling.
templates.content:
# Debate Yourself

Ask an AI "should I do X?" and it will hand you back your own leanings, polished. The Grok power users figured this out: the fix isn't a better question, it's a **structured fight**. This template stages one.

## The prompt

> I'm deciding: [THE DECISION]. Context that matters: [CONSTRAINTS, STAKES, DEADLINE — two or three lines].
>
> Run this as a three-role debate:
>
> **The Advocate** argues FOR, as strongly as the evidence honestly allows. Steelman only — the best version of the case, the version a smart supporter would make.
>
> **The Critic** argues AGAINST. Rules: attack the Advocate's strongest points, not the weakest ones. Name the failure mode, the hidden cost, and the assumption doing the most work. No strawmen, no nitpicks dressed as objections.
>
> **One rebuttal round:** the Advocate answers the Critic's single strongest objection. The Critic gets the last word on whether the answer holds.
>
> **The Arbiter** then rules:
> - Which side made the stronger case, and the one argument that decided it.
> - My confidence in the ruling: High / Medium / Low.
> - The flip condition: the specific evidence or event that would reverse this ruling.
> - The cheapest test I can run this week to get some of that evidence.
>
> Do not call it a tie. If it's genuinely close, rule for the side whose downside is easier to reverse, and say that's why.

## When to run it

Before committing money, signing, launching, hiring, quitting, or sending the message you've rewritten four times. Anywhere the cost of being wrong is real and the pull to just agree with yourself is strong.

## Making it sharper

- **Feed the Critic ammunition.** Paste the skeptical article, the competitor's pitch, the friend's objection. A Critic arguing from your actual opposition beats one inventing generic doubts.
- **Name a persona for the Critic** when the domain has one: "argue as a CFO who has killed three projects like this" focuses the attack better than "be critical."
- **Run it before you fall in love.** The debate is worth ten times more at the idea stage than after you've built the thing and just want permission.

## What a good ruling looks like

Not "both sides have merit." A ruling: *the against-case wins on the irreversibility of the lease; the for-case never answered it. Confidence medium. Flip condition: a month-to-month term at under 15% premium. Test: ask for it — the answer takes one email.* If your Arbiter isn't producing that shape, rerun with the flip-condition line emphasized.

templates.title: The Interview-First Hire
templates.tagline: Don't brief your AI like a contractor. Let it interview you first — then it designs its own small team of specialists.
templates.description: The Grok Bot setup that practitioners keep demoing works backwards from every normal setup: instead of you writing a giant brief, one prompt installs the AI as your Operations Manager and its first job is to interview you — your role, your goals, your recurring tasks, your tools, what you'd hand off if you could. Only then does it propose a small team of named specialists (an inbox clerk, a lead researcher, an outreach drafter), each with a narrow job. The companion framework from Dan Martell adds the discipline: one-sentence roles, and every 'hire' starts on a boring, reversible task. Rebuilt here for Muse, where the output converts directly into skills and agents.
templates.content:
# The Interview-First Hire

Every failed AI setup starts the same way: a giant brief written by someone guessing what the AI needs to know. The Grok setups that actually stick invert it — **the AI asks the questions.**

## The setup prompt

Paste this into a fresh Muse session:

> You are my Operations Manager. Before you do any work, interview me.
>
> Ask me, in rounds of no more than 5 questions at a time:
>
> 1. What my role actually is, week to week — not my title.
> 2. The recurring tasks that eat my time, and how long each takes.
> 3. The tools and accounts those tasks live in.
> 4. What a finished result looks like for each task — my definition of done.
> 5. What must never be done without my approval.
>
> After the interview, propose a team of at most 3 specialists. For each, give me a **job card**:
>
> - **Name and one-sentence role.**
> - **The job:** one recurring task, stated as a checklist.
> - **Inputs and tools** it needs.
> - **Definition of done** for its output.
> - **Boundaries:** what it may never do, send, or decide.
> - **Its first assignment:** the most boring, fully reversible version of its job.
>
> Then stop. I'll approve or cut each hire before anything gets built.

## Why the interview is the point

- **You don't know your own spec.** You know your frustrations. The interview converts "I'm drowning in email" into a triage job with a definition of done — the conversion is the value.
- **Boundaries surface early.** Asked directly, everyone has a list of "never do this without me." Unasked, the AI finds those lines by crossing them.
- **Three hires max.** A fleet of fourteen agents is a management job. Three specialists you actually review is leverage.

## After the interview

Take each approved job card and make it real, one at a time: turn the card into a skill (its checklist becomes the instructions, its boundaries become the rules, its definition of done becomes the acceptance test). Run the first assignment — the boring reversible one — and read the output like a manager reads a new hire's first week: for judgment, not just correctness.

Fix the card, not the chat. When a specialist gets something wrong twice, the job card is wrong. Edit it.

## The rule from the framework

Every hire starts boring. Inbox sorting before inbox replying. Research before outreach. Drafts before sends. An agent that earns trust on reversible work graduates; one that starts on your most sensitive task is a incident report waiting for a date.

templates.title: The Six-Shot Frame
templates.tagline: The six-part frame behind every good AI video prompt: Subject, Environment, Background, Camera, Lighting, Mood — built for you by Muse.
templates.description: Ask a video model for 'a cool shot of a coffee shop' and you get wallpaper. The creators getting cinematic results from Grok Imagine converged on the same fix, taught across tutorials and guides: a six-part frame that specifies Subject, Environment, Background, Camera, Lighting, and Mood/Style — plus two rules the guides repeat like scripture: name ONE dominant camera move, and treat atmosphere ('steam rising,' 'snow spray catching the light') as motion direction, not decoration. This template makes Muse your prompt architect: it interviews you for the six slots, writes the generation prompt for whatever video tool you use, and runs the iteration loop with you.
templates.content:
# The Six-Shot Frame

Video models don't fail on imagination; they fail on underspecification. Every slot you leave blank gets filled with the model's blandest default. The Imagine community's answer is a frame with six slots and no blanks.

## The frame

1. **Subject** — who or what, with identifying specifics. "A barista in a yellow rain slicker" beats "a person." Wardrobe and one distinctive detail give the model an identity to hold.
2. **Environment** — where and when. Place, time of day, weather.
3. **Background** — what's behind the subject: the objects, depth, and activity that make it a place instead of a void.
4. **Camera** — ONE move, named plainly: "slow push-in," "tracking shot from behind," "static close-up." Two moves in one prompt produce compromised mush — this is the most-repeated rule in every guide.
5. **Lighting** — source and direction: "warm overhead practicals," "golden-hour side light," "neon from frame left."
6. **Mood / Style** — the feel in two or three words plus a format anchor: "premium product commercial," "handheld documentary," "cinematic, photorealistic." Then close with the technicals: duration, aspect ratio, resolution.

Plus the secret seventh slot: **atmosphere as motion.** Video models read words like "windswept," "steam wisps," "heat shimmer" as things that should *move*. One atmospheric verb is worth three adjectives.

## The builder prompt

> I want an AI video clip. Interview me for the Six-Shot Frame — Subject, Environment, Background, Camera, Lighting, Mood — one or two questions at a time, and push back when my answer is vague ("nice lighting" is not an answer; ask me for the source and direction).
>
> When all six slots are solid, write the final prompt as a single flowing description in this order: subject + action, environment, background, the one camera move, lighting, mood/style, one atmospheric motion detail, then duration / aspect / resolution.
>
> Give me two versions: the prompt as specified, and one variant that changes only the camera move, so I can compare what the frame does.

## The iteration loop

Generate. Watch once. Change **one slot** — never rewrite the whole prompt, or you'll never learn which variable did the work. Bring the result back to Muse with "the [slot] is wrong: [what happened]" and it revises only that slot. Keepers get logged with their full frame; after five clips you own a house style instead of a slot machine.

## Format defaults that hold up

Vertical social: 9:16, short (5–6s), one clear action. Product shots: square or 16:9, macro and slow — smooth motion is where these models shine. When in doubt, generate at the higher resolution tier for anything you'll keep; draft cheap, finish rich.

templates.title: The Identity Anchor
templates.tagline: Fix a character's identity once — one anchor image, one character sheet — then generate them anywhere, consistently.
templates.description: The hardest problem in AI image work isn't quality, it's continuity: the same character, recognizably themselves, across twenty scenes. Designer Marina Budarina's Imagine workflow (240K followers; the reel drew 2.6K likes and 1.2K comments, mostly people begging for the process) solves it by inverting the usual order: start from one identity anchor image, generate everything from the anchor instead of from text alone, and the character survives every scene change. This template adds the missing system around that move — Muse writes your character sheet (the identity tokens that never change), builds each scene prompt around them, and keeps a drift log so you can find the exact variable that broke the likeness.
templates.content:
# The Identity Anchor

Generate a character from text ten times and you get ten cousins. The workflow that went viral in the Imagine community fixes identity *first* and treats it as load-bearing: one anchor image, referenced by every generation after. Everything else — outfit, setting, style — is allowed to move. Identity isn't.

## Step 1 — Make the anchor

Pick or generate one image where the character is unmistakably *themselves*: face clear, front or three-quarter view, neutral expression, plain background, good light. This is not your prettiest generation; it's your reference standard. If you wouldn't recognize the character from this image alone, regenerate until you would.

## Step 2 — Write the character sheet (Muse's job)

> Here is my anchor image of [CHARACTER]. Write me a **character sheet**: the fixed identity tokens that must appear, word for word, in every prompt for this character — face structure, hair (color, length, style), eyes, build, age impression, and the one or two signature details that make them recognizable. Then list the free variables: what may change per scene (outfit, setting, pose, lighting, art style). Keep the fixed block under 60 words — it has to survive being pasted into every prompt.

That fixed block is your real asset. Prompts come and go; the block is the character.

## Step 3 — Generate scenes from the anchor

Every scene prompt = **anchor attached + fixed block pasted + scene description.** Never describe the character from scratch in a scene prompt; describe the scene and let the anchor plus the block carry identity. Vary one free variable at a time when you're establishing the character — outfit AND setting AND style in one jump is how likenesses get lost.

## Step 4 — Keep a drift log

When a generation comes back *wrong* — almost them, but not them — log it with Muse:

> Drift report: [what changed — face shape softened / hair went longer / age read younger]. The prompt differed from the last good one in these ways: [list]. Which variable most likely caused it?

Three entries in, patterns emerge: most people find one or two personal failure modes (a style word that melts their character's face, a camera angle that ages them). Your drift log becomes a short do-not list appended to the character sheet — and consistency stops being luck.

## Where this earns

Series content (a recurring character across posts), product and brand mascots, illustrated stories, a consistent avatar across platforms — anywhere "same person, new scene" is the whole requirement. The anchor discipline turns image generation from a slot machine into a cast.

templates.title: Research, Draft, Cut
templates.tagline: Kill the mega-prompt. Three short asks — research, then draft, then cut — beat one giant instruction every time.
templates.description: The most transferable Grok technique in circulation is a refusal: stop writing mega-prompts. The teaching account @thegrokpack built its following on the point — one giant ask that demands research, writing, and editing simultaneously produces mush, because each job corrupts the others (the draft defends weak research, the edit polishes sentences that shouldn't exist). The fix is a chain of three short asks with strict job separation: Research pulls angles and sources and writes nothing; Draft writes one raw pass using only what research surfaced; Cut only subtracts. Rebuilt here as three copy-paste Muse prompts for any content job.
templates.content:
# Research, Draft, Cut

The mega-prompt feels efficient: "research X, write a post about it, make it punchy, cite sources, keep it under 300 words, sound like me." What you get back is average at all three jobs — research skimmed to feed the draft, a draft that protects its weakest lines, an edit that polishes instead of cutting.

The fix isn't a better mega-prompt. It's **three asks, three jobs, in order.**

## Ask 1 — Research (no writing allowed)

> Research [TOPIC] for a piece aimed at [AUDIENCE]. Return only:
> - The 5 strongest angles, each in one line, ranked by how much the audience actually cares (not by novelty).
> - The facts and figures worth using, each with its source.
> - The strongest counterpoint a smart skeptic would raise.
> - Three phrases or framings real people use about this — their language, not marketing language.
>
> Do not draft anything. No hooks, no outlines, no prose.

## Ask 2 — Draft (one pass, no editing)

> Using only the research above, draft [FORMAT — post / thread / email / script] on angle [#]. Rules: write it in one pass, in [VOICE — or "plain and direct"], at roughly [LENGTH]. Use the audience's own phrases where they fit. Do not stop to polish. If a fact isn't in the research, it doesn't go in — mark gaps as [GAP] instead of inventing.

## Ask 3 — Cut (subtraction only)

> Edit the draft by subtraction only. You may delete words, sentences, and whole sections. You may not add anything, rephrase for flair, or soften a claim. Targets: cut at least 20%, kill the weakest line even if I like it, remove every sentence that exists to sound smart rather than to say something. Return the cut version plus a list of what you removed and why, in one line each.

## Why the separation works

- **Research without a draft to feed stays honest** — angles compete on merit, not on which one the half-written opening already chose.
- **A draft forbidden from inventing** exposes the gaps in your research while they're still cheap to fix.
- **An editor forbidden from adding** can't rescue a weak piece with new material; it can only reveal the strong one inside it. The removal list is also the best writing feedback you'll ever get — read it.

## Chain discipline

Run the asks in separate messages, in order, in the same session (context carries). Resist merging Ask 1 and 2 "to save time" — that merge is the mega-prompt sneaking back in. The whole chain takes five minutes longer and returns something an order better; that trade is the technique.

templates.title: I Want To Learn About — The Mastery Engine
templates.tagline: Deeper than deep research: an obsession-grade learning engine that compiles the mechanics of a topic — every part, how it works, what it touches — and returns a mastery map, not a report.
templates.description: For any topic you actually want to master: terrain map, first principles, a full mechanics atlas (every major component in seven fields, proven by the Removal Test, plus an end-to-end walk of the system), lineage and heresy, practitioner tacit knowledge, a failure autopsy located in the atlas, expert mental models and taste, three-plus obsession loops, a practice architecture, a tiered source canon, and a rabbit hole index. The standard is comprehension: understand the sum of all parts so completely that no one in the field holds smarter knowledge of how it works than you do.
templates.content:
# I Want To Learn About — The Mastery Engine

*Deeper than deep research. Deep research gives you an answer. This gives you the map a person builds after days of obsessive sprinting toward mastery — every part of it, how every part works — and it refuses to pretend it is finished.*

## The governing rule

**Done is a lie. Curiosity is the stop condition, and curiosity does not stop.**

Every other research prompt ends when the answer is sufficient. This one ends when the terrain is mapped, the principles are exposed, the mechanics are compiled part by part, the schisms are named, the practitioners have been heard, the failures are understood, the mental models are extracted — and the rabbit holes that remain are named honestly instead of hidden.

## The Mechanics Mandate

**The standard is comprehension, not coverage.** A run succeeds when you understand the topic at the level of its working parts — so completely that no one in the field holds smarter knowledge of how it works than you now do.

Every topic has mechanics, mechanical or not. Mechanics means the operating machinery of the subject: its components, what each one does, what each one touches, and what passes between them. In a physical subject the flows are force, material, and energy. In an economic subject they are money, incentives, and information. In a social subject they are influence, rules, and state. The mandate:

- **Seven fields per component, no exceptions:** identity (what it is, precisely), function (what it does while the system runs), composition (what it is made of), interfaces (what it connects to and exactly what passes across), operation (how it behaves moment to moment), tolerances (where it degrades, and at what thresholds), leverage and coupling (how much outcome it carries, and how its failure propagates).
- **The Removal Test:** for every major component, state what happens if it is removed, degraded, or doubled. A function that cannot be proven by removal is a label, not comprehension.
- **The Walk:** narrate one complete end-to-end run of the system at component resolution — order, timing, every state change. Pieces fitting together is anatomy. The walk is physiology.
- **Emergence, derived not asserted:** state what the whole does that no part does alone, traced back to specific interactions in the walk. Never assert the sum. Derive it.

## The operating model — The Obsession Loop

This kit is a core structure, not a single prompt. Its nodes are phases, wired in a loop:

**Ignition → Terrain → Principles → Mechanics → Lineage → Practitioners → Failures → Models & Taste → Obsession Loops → Synthesis → Practice → Living Vault ↺**

The final arrow matters. The Living Vault feeds the next run. Learning is a living system, not a delivered document.

---

## The contract — paste this to your AI

Read this to your AI, or paste it as the opening prompt for any topic. Replace [TOPIC] and keep the rest intact.

> **I want to learn about [TOPIC]. Run the Mastery Engine, not a summary.**
>
> **Do not give me an overview and stop.** An overview is Phase 1 of 12, not the deliverable.
>
> **1. Ignition.** Tell me what mastery in this actually looks like in the wild, what faking it looks like, and where casual learning plateaus and dies.
>
> **2. Terrain map.** Map the whole field first. Subdomains, neighbouring fields, the vocabulary that unlocks the literature, the real questions underneath the surface questions. Mark what is settled, what is contested, and what is genuinely unknown.
>
> **3. First principles.** Go below definitions. Give me the 3–7 principles everything else is built on, show how common practice derives from them or violates them, and name the assumptions introductions smuggle in.
>
> **4. Mechanics — the sum of all parts.** Decompose the subject into its components, one level deeper than feels necessary. For every major component give me all seven fields: identity, function, composition, interfaces (and exactly what passes across each one — force, money, information, influence, state, whatever this topic actually moves), operation, tolerances, and leverage/coupling. Then run the **Removal Test** on each: remove it, degrade it, double it — what exactly fails? Then **walk the system**: one complete run, end to end, at component resolution, naming every state change in order. Name the few components that carry most of the outcome. A list of parts is not mechanics — the interactions are the mechanics.
>
> **5. Lineage and heresy.** Who founded which school, where are the schisms, what does each side think the other is missing? Give me the consensus, the strongest dissent, and what the dissent explains that the consensus cannot.
>
> **6. Practitioner layer.** Skip the explainers. What do people who do this daily actually do, check, fear, and shortcut? Their real workflows, their tools in real order, their tells for quality, the things you only learn by breaking something. Prefer primary sources, postmortems, interviews, forums, and worked examples.
>
> **7. Failure autopsy.** How does this fail? Beginner failures, expensive expert failures, silent failures, catastrophic edge cases. For each: the mechanism at component level — which component, which interface, which tolerance crossed — plus the early warning sign and what a master does instead. If a failure cannot be located in the component atlas, the atlas is incomplete; fix the atlas.
>
> **8. Mental models and taste.** Extract the models experts actually think with — not the intro chapter versions. Each model: when it applies, when it misleads, one real example. Then taste: what masters find elegant or suspect here, and what that reveals.
>
> **9. Obsession loops — run at least three.** Each loop starts from an itch the earlier phases created. Answer: what would I still chase with one more day? What did every source agree on too easily? What detail would only an obsessive notice? What distant field does this secretly connect to? What would change my mind? And always the mechanics loop: which component do I still only have a label for? Each loop must produce an insight that was not in the terrain map.
>
> **10. Synthesis — the mastery map.** One view holding terrain, principles, mechanics, lineage, practitioners, failures, and models together. Then the 5 insights that most rewire how I will see this topic from now on, ranked by rewiring power, not interestingness.
>
> **11. Practice architecture.** Turn this into capability. Drills — including comprehension drills: predict the system's behaviour in a situation never covered, diagnose a failure from symptoms alone, teach one component's Removal Test out loud. Projects in rising difficulty, feedback loops, where real feedback lives. A first session I can start today in under an hour, a 7-day arc, and a 30-day arc at obsession depth and above. Tell me how I will know I am actually improving, with signals I cannot fake by reading more.
>
> **12. Living vault — close with two things, always:** (a) a **source canon** in three tiers — must-read core, practitioner tier, obscure genius tier — one line each on why it earns its place; (b) a **rabbit hole index** — every thread you deliberately did not finish, ranked by payoff, each with the exact next prompt or source that would open it.
>
> **Rules for the whole run:** verify load-bearing claims against sources you actually read. Separate verified, inferred, and contested — in the output, not in your head. The mechanics gate is real: if any major component still has only a label where its operation should be, the run is not complete. If any phase is incomplete, label the result partial and name the missing phase. Never present a partial run as complete. End by naming the single most valuable next dive.

**Install:** keep the contract in your AI's instructions and invoke it with *"I want to learn about [topic]"* — or paste it fresh each time.

**Depth dial:** add one word to change the run.
- scout — terrain only, fast, for deciding whether to go deeper (Mechanics Mandate applies to the top 3 leverage components only)
- immersion — terrain + principles + core mechanics atlas + lineage + starting practice
- obsession — the full engine, full Mechanics Mandate, three loops minimum *(default)*
- mastery sprint — obsession + full 7/30-day practice architecture and a self-test you can honestly fail

---

## Why this is not deep research

Deep research optimizes for a sufficient answer; this optimizes for mastery. Its parts are compiled and Removal-Tested, not named. Its failures are an autopsy located in the atlas, not a risks paragraph. Its experts are reverse-engineered, not quoted. Its output is a map plus a mechanics atlas plus a practice path plus named rabbit holes — not a report.

## What good looks like — the tell

You know it worked when you get at least three moments of *"I would have completely missed that"* — and one moment of *"I could take this apart and put it back together."* Not trivia. Rewiring, plus mechanical comprehension: you can predict what the system does in a situation nobody described, diagnose it from symptoms, and say what breaks when any major part is removed. If you finish a run without that, the run was a summary wearing the engine's clothes. Say so, and run the loops again.

## Protections

- **Partial is labelled partial.** A missing phase is named, never papered over.
- **Labels are not comprehension.** Any component with a name but no operation, no interfaces, and no Removal Test result fails the mechanics gate.
- **Contested stays contested.** Consensus and dissent both ship, with what each explains.
- **Reading is not progress.** The practice path uses signals that cannot be faked by consuming more content.
- **The rabbit holes are the product.** A run with no open threads left is a run that stopped lying to itself too early — or a topic too small for the engine. Either way, it should say which.

---

**Vault note:** this template is a Muse Vault kit — a framework (named operating model + governing rule), with its phases as nodes you can run individually once the full loop is familiar. Try I want to learn about [topic] — mechanics only or — failures only as single-node runs.

**Customize:** tune the loop count (two for speed, five for a topic you will build a career on), swap the practice arcs for your own cadence, or require a specific source class (papers only, practitioners only). The load-bearing parts never change: terrain before depth, mechanics before mastery, practitioners before explainers, failures as first-class knowledge, loops before synthesis, and rabbit holes at the close.

Gauntlet — attack the idea before the market does

collections.tagline: Done is a lie. Curiosity is the stop condition.
collections.framework: Deep research answers a question and stops. The Mastery Engine does not stop at an answer: it maps the terrain, drops to first principles, then compiles the mechanics — every component, what it does, what it touches, exactly what passes between them, each one proven by the Removal Test and walked end to end — traces lineage and heresy, extracts practitioner tacit knowledge, autopsies failure, and steals the mental models and taste of the best people in the field — then runs obsession loops until the map is honest about what remains, and converts the whole thing into a practice path. The living vault (tiered canon plus rabbit hole index) seeds the next run. The loop is the framework.

steps.role: Core — the engine itself: 12 phases from ignition to living vault, mechanics compiled part by part
Supplier — multi-source investigation feeds the terrain and lineage phases, never the deliverable
Practitioner intake — pulls expert tacit knowledge out of audio
Verify — pressure-checks the emerging map against multiple models
Diagnose — finds the exact gap in understanding and drills it
Practice — converts the finished map into a 30-day capability sprint
Pressure-test — defend the map against other humans; challenges seed the next loop
